sec.title: Background
sec.p: Definitive chemoradiotherapy is a standard treatment for unresectable locally advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (LAESCC), but complete response rates remain 15%-25%, and median overall survival (OS) is 13-14 months. More effective strategies are needed.

sec.title: Trial design
sec.p: The PALADIN trial is a nonrandomized, single-arm phase II study evaluating the efficacy and safety of induction pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy with short-course radiotherapy (SCRT) in unresectable LAESCC. Eligible patients have confirmed squamous cell carcinoma with T3br-T4b (Japanese Classification of Esophageal Cancer, 12th edition). Treatment consists of pembrolizumab 200 mg and cisplatin 80 mg/m2 IV day 1, and continuous 5-fluorouracil 800 mg/m2/day on days 1-5 every 3 weeks for four cycles, with SCRT of 25 Gy in five fractions on days 8-12 of cycle 1. After study treatment, patients eligible for R0 resection will undergo subtotal esophagectomy with 2- or 3-field lymph node dissection. The primary endpoint is 2-year OS. Exploratory endpoints include analysis of molecular residual disease using a personalized, tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA assay (SignateraTM, Natera, Inc., Austin, TX) and translational studies. Planned enrollment is 35 patients, assuming a threshold 2-year OS rate of 30% and an expected rate of 50%, with one-sided α of 0.10 and 80% power.
Key words: unresectable locally advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy with short-course radiotherapy, induction treatment

list-item.p: PALADIN evaluates induction pembrolizumab plus fluorouracil and cisplatin with short-course radiotherapy for unresectable LAESCC.
The trial aims to improve 2-year OS and enable conversion surgery with an immuno-radiotherapy strategy.
Exploratory analyses include personalized tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA molecular residual disease assessment to predict recurrence and treatment response.

sec.p: Collection date 2026 Jun.

sec.title: Background and rationale
sec.p: Definitive chemoradiotherapy (dCRT) is one of the standard treatments for unresectable locally advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (LAESCC), but the complete response (CR) rate remains low at 15%-25%, and median overall survival (OS) is only 13-14 months,1,2 highlighting the need for more effective strategies. According to the National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines, chemotherapy is another treatment option, especially for patients with unresectable LAESCC involving the trachea, great vessels, vertebral body, or heart.3 Recent randomized phase III trials have demonstrated the survival benefit of anti-programmed cell death protein-1 antibodies plus chemotherapy over chemotherapy alone in patients with unresectable esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, including locally advanced disease.4, 5, 6 In addition, basic research and preclinical studies have suggested that short-course radiotherapy (SCRT) may induce a synergistic effect in combination with immunotherapy, compared with conventionally fractionated radiotherapy.7, 8, 9

sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: This trial explores whether induction treatment of pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy with SCRT can improve long-term outcomes in patients with unresectable LAESCC. We also conduct translational research, including evaluation of molecular residual disease (MRD) using a personalized, tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) assay.

sec.title: Trial design and treatment
sec.p: The PALADIN trial is a nonrandomized, single-arm, phase II trial (Figures 1, 2 and Table 1). Patients receive pembrolizumab 200 mg i.v. on day 1, cisplatin 80 mg/m2 i.v. on day 1, and 5-fluorouracil 800 mg/m2/day by continuous infusion on days 1-5 every 3 weeks (FP) for four cycles, with SCRT of 25 Gy in five fractions administered on days 8-12 of cycle 1. Tumor response will be assessed using computed tomography (CT) and endoscopy according to the RECIST (version 1.1),10 with CT evaluating overall tumor burden and endoscopy assessing local esophageal response, at two timepoints: after two cycles and after completion of four cycles. Patients considered eligible for R0 resection based on the second evaluation will proceed to subtotal esophagectomy with 2- or 3-field lymph node dissection. Patients who successfully undergo conversion surgery will be considered to have completed the protocol treatment. Protocol treatment will be discontinued in case of confirmed disease progression, unacceptable toxicities, or unresectability after induction therapy (Table 2). Post-operative adjuvant therapy is administered at the discretion of the treating physician; however, in nonpathological complete response (pCR) cases, continuation of an immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) for up to 1 year at the discretion of the treating physician is recommended.

caption.p: Study design of the PALADIN trial. The PALADIN trial is a single-arm phase II study evaluating pembrolizumab plus fluorouracil and cisplatin (FP) combined with short-course radiotherapy (SCRT) as induction treatment for patients with unresectable locally advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (cT3br–4b, Nany, M0) without prior therapy. Patients receive four cycles of pembrolizumab plus FP chemotherapy with concurrent SCRT (25 Gy in five fractions), followed by surgery when feasible. Adjuvant immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy for up to 1 year is allowed in patients without pathological complete response. The primary endpoint is the 2-year overall survival rate. Secondary endpoints include R0 resection rate, pathological response, progression-free survival, overall survival, and safety. Exploratory analyses include circulating tumor DNA assessment and translational research. ICI, immune checkpoint inhibitor; pCR, pathological complete response.

Schema of tissue sampling. Tumor tissue biopsies are collected at predefined time points to enable pathological assessment and exploratory translational analyses. CT, computed tomography; EGD, esophagogastroduodenoscopy; SCRT, short-course radiotherapy.

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: The eligibility criteria are listed in Table 3. The major eligibility criteria are as follows: histologically confirmed diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma; T3br (possible adjacent organ invasion; aorta, trachea, bronchus, pulmonary vein/artery, or vertebral body), T4a, or T4b (Japanese Classification of Esophageal Cancer, 12th edition) without distant metastasis, or T1-T3 deemed unresectable due to regional or supraclavicular lymph node metastasis; age ≥18 years; Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0 or 1; presence of sufficient organ function; and obtained written informed consent.

sec.title: Follow-up
sec.p: Follow-up evaluations on CT scans and tumor markers (carcinoembryonic antigen and squamous cell carcinoma) will be conducted every 3 months after surgery and continued until 2 years from the date of enrollment. After that, follow-up evaluations are recommended every 6 months until disease progression or up to 5 years after enrollment. Post-operative treatments, including ICI use, are not mandated by the protocol but will be recorded as part of posttreatment data collection.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary endpoint of this study is the 2-year OS rate, defined as the proportion of patients who remain alive at 2 years from the date of enrollment. Secondary endpoints include the R0 resection rate, pCR rate, major pathological response rate, progression-free survival, OS, distant metastasis–free survival, patterns and rates of recurrence, the incidence of adverse events, and the incidence of perioperative complications, assessed by the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v5.0. Perioperative safety will also be evaluated for intraoperative and surgical complications using both CTCAE v5.0 and the Clavien–Dindo classification v2.0.

sec.title: Planned sample size and study period
sec.p: A total of 35 patients are planned to be enrolled. The enrollment period commenced in July 2025 and is expected to continue until June 2027. The follow-up period will last 2 years after completion of enrollment, and the entire trial period is scheduled to conclude in June 2030.

sec.title: Statistical methods
sec.p: Previous studies have reported that the 2- or 3-year OS rate for unresectable LAESCC is ∼20%-30%.1,2 In this trial, the threshold 2-year OS rate was set at 30%, with an expected improvement of 20% in the survival rate with the investigational treatment, resulting in an expected value of 50%. Assuming a one-sided significance level of 10% (α = 0.10) and a power of 80% (β = 0.20), the required sample size calculated based on a binomial distribution was 32 patients. Given the potential for dropouts, the total sample size was set at 35 patients.

sec.title: Exploratory analyses
sec.p: MRD will be assessed using a personalized, tumor-informed ctDNA assay (SignateraTM, Natera, Inc.).11 Briefly, whole-exome sequencing (WES) will be carried out on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embeddded tumor tissue from surgically resected primary tumors and matched normal blood samples. Based on WES results, up to 16 patient-specific somatic single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) will be selected for downstream plasma-based ctDNA testing. Plasma samples with ≥2 SNVs detected out of 16 will be considered ctDNA positive, and the concentration will be reported in mean tumor molecules per milliliter (mL) of plasma. Plasma samples for ctDNA assessment will be collected at baseline, postinduction, and postsurgery. Data ownership and analysis responsibilities between National Cancer Center Hospital East and Natera are governed by a formal research collaboration agreement.
Tumor samples obtained before, during, and after treatment are subjected to translational analyses, including programmed death-ligand 1 expression, WES, and whole-transcriptome sequencing.

sec.title: Protocol validation
sec.p: In patients with unresectable LAESCC, dCRT is administered with curative intent; however, the CR rate remains low at ∼15%-25%. In addition, the median OS remains ∼13-14 months. These outcomes highlight the need for novel treatment strategies that achieve durable control of both locoregional and distant disease.

Regarding induction strategies, the phase II COSMOS trial demonstrated the efficacy and safety of induction DCF (docetaxel, cisplatin, and 5-fluorouracil) followed by conversion surgery in patients with unresectable LAESCC.12 Based on these results, the ongoing phase III JCOG1510 is comparing induction DCF with dCRT.13 In contrast, another randomized phase II trial (n = 101) comparing induction chemoradiotherapy (CRT) versus induction DCF highlighted the importance of radiotherapy (RT) for effective local control and survival improvement for unresectable LAESCC (cT4b); a favorable trend in 2-year OS for the CRT group (55.1% versus 34.7%, P = 0.11), although not statistically significant.14 While R0 resection rates were similar (∼77%) and distant metastasis tended to be less frequent with DCF, induction CRT significantly reduced locoregional recurrence (local: 8% versus 30%, P = 0.03; regional: 8% versus 37%, P = 0.002).

From the perspective of distant disease control, effective systemic chemotherapy is essential. In the randomized phase III KEYNOTE-590 trial, pembrolizumab plus FP was established as a standard of care, showing a significant improvement in OS compared with placebo plus FP; notably, ∼10% of enrolled patients had unresectable locally advanced disease.4 Similarly, the phase III CheckMate 648 trial showed the efficacy of nivolumab plus FP, with subgroup analysis suggesting a survival benefit in locally advanced disease (hazard ratio 0.73).5 In contrast, the DCF regimen failed to demonstrate survival superiority over FP in the metastatic setting (phase III JCOG1314).15 Based on these findings, FP plus pembrolizumab, which has demonstrated superiority over FP alone with respect to distant disease control, was selected as the systemic therapy backbone for the PALADIN trial.

With respect to the combination of RT and ICIs, maximizing synergy is critical. While sequential ICI following RT has shown efficacy in phase III trials,16, 17, 18 concurrent RT and ICI strategies have yielded mixed results.19 Aside from the positive results in the phase III KEYNOTE-A18 trial in cervical cancer,20 other concurrent trials (e.g. JAVELIN Head and Neck 100, KEYNOTE-412, PACIFIC2) have failed to show benefit,21, 22, 23 potentially due to lymphocyte depletion caused by prolonged conventional fractionation and elective nodal irradiation.9,19 Accordingly, minimizing lymphocyte depletion is critical. Preclinical studies and the iSABR trial in lung cancer suggested that hypofractionated RT (increasing dose per fraction while shortening duration) may enhance immunogenic synergy.6,7 Based on this rationale, the PALADIN trial adopts SCRT (25 Gy in five fractions) without elective nodal irradiation to preserve lymphocyte counts and maximize the synergistic effect with concurrent pembrolizumab.

Beyond considerations of efficacy, safety is a paramount concern. One major concern is the increased risk of interstitial pneumonitis (IP). Previous studies suggested that reducing the total radiation dose may lower the incidence of IP.24,25 By adopting SCRT, this trial aims to mitigate IP risk while maintaining local efficacy. Moreover, since salvage surgery after high-dose radiation carries substantial risks,26 the dose reduction in this setting is also anticipated to improve surgical safety.

In summary, the PALADIN trial explores a novel induction strategy for unresectable LAESCC by integrating pembrolizumab-based systemic therapy with concurrent SCRT. This approach aims to achieve robust local control while preserving immunological synergy and ensuring surgical feasibility. In addition, incorporating ctDNA-based MRD assessment may provide translational insights into treatment response and recurrence risk, informing future multimodal strategies for this challenging disease.
